opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of the disagreement here comes from people using "meaning" to refer to quite different things, so I usually start by splitting the question apart.

One version is the classic grounding worry: these models are trained only on text, never touch the world, so how could the symbols they manipulate be *about* anything? There's a strong version of that argument that I don't find persuasive. It's not obvious that you need direct perceptual contact for representations to carry information about the world, because text is produced by people who *do* have that contact. Text is a very rich, if indirect, signal about the states of the world and the beliefs of the people writing it. A model trying to predict text well has a real incentive to recover some of that underlying structure.

So the more productive question to me is empirical. Instead of asking "does it understand?", we can ask: are there internal representations that systematically track things like the state of the world described by a discourse, the truth conditions of a sentence, or the beliefs and goals of the speaker? Can we find them with probes, and, more importantly, can we intervene on them and get predictable changes in behavior? When you do that kind of experiment, say with a model reading a story about objects moving between containers, you do often find something that looks like an implicit, if imperfect and somewhat fragile, model of the situation being described. That doesn't settle the philosophy, but it moves the conversation from intuition pumps to evidence.

One framing I've found useful is thinking of language models as models of *agents*, or of the communicative intentions behind text. Any given document was written by someone with particular beliefs and goals. A good predictor of text has to implicitly infer something about who is speaking and what they're trying to do. Seen that way, the question isn't whether the model has one coherent worldview, because it probably doesn't. It's whether, in context, it can represent the beliefs of the agent who would have produced this text. Sometimes it does that well, and a lot of the familiar failures, like incoherence or inconsistency across prompts, make sense once you see the model as juggling many possible speakers at once.

So my short answer is that "no meaning at all" is too strong, and "they understand language the way we do" is also too strong. They clearly build some meaning-like representations, sometimes surprisingly structured ones, but they're partial, often not robust, and not organized the way we'd want if we expected a single consistent model of the world. The interesting scientific work is mapping exactly where those representations exist, where they break, and what training signals or architectures would make them more coherent.

r002.rationale: It discusses text as an indirect signal about the world, but does not explain a model-theoretic account using possible worlds without real-world grounding.

r003.rationale: It does not describe a proof-theoretic account or say that recognizing relationships between sentences can suffice for meaning.

r004.rationale: It mentions authors’ beliefs and goals, but does not locate linguistic meaning in a community’s history of interactions.

r005.rationale: It proposes empirical questions about representations, but does not state that making a conception of meaning precise generally makes a corresponding model question relatively straightforward to formulate.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that it depends a lot on what you mean by "meaning," and a lot of the disagreement in the field comes from people using the word in different ways.

There's a classic argument, which Emily Bender and Alexander Koller made nicely a few years ago, that a model trained only on text can't learn meaning because it never has access to the things the words refer to. If meaning is reference, a connection between the word "cup" and actual cups in the world, then a model that's only ever seen text has no way to acquire that. And I think that version of the argument is basically right as far as it goes.

But I don't think reference is the only thing meaning is. A lot of what we mean when we say someone understands a word is that they know how it relates to other words, what inferences it licenses, what situations it describes and how those situations evolve. And text carries a surprising amount of that. If you read enough descriptions of people moving around rooms, you can build a pretty good internal model of rooms and movement even without ever having been in one. So there's an empirical question lurking here, which is: when you train these models on text, what kind of internal structure do they actually build?

That's where a lot of my own work has gone. In the probing and interpretability experiments we've done, you can find cases where a model trained on, say, descriptions of a board game or a simple text adventure ends up with internal representations that track the state of the world being described. Not just the surface of the text, but something like the entities, their properties, and how they change as the text proceeds. You can read those states out, and you can intervene on them and change what the model says next in ways that are consistent with having edited the world state. That looks a lot like what we'd want a representation of meaning to do.

So my view is that the question "do language models represent meaning?" isn't really a yes-or-no question. It's better to ask what specific pieces of the machinery of meaning they've acquired, which ones are missing, and how we'd know. They clearly have something. They clearly don't have everything, particularly the grounding part. And the interesting work is in making those claims precise enough that you could actually run an experiment and be wrong.

r003.rationale: It mentions word relationships and inferences, but does not explain a proof-theoretic account where recognizing relationships between sentences is sufficient for meaning.

r004.rationale: It does not describe meaning as arising from a community’s history of interactions.

astra-6.text:
I think we have to unpack what we mean by meaning. One question is whether a language model is just keeping track of superficial properties of strings, or whether it has representations of the things those strings describe—objects, events, relationships. Another question is whether those representations are grounded in the world in the same way that human representations are. Those are different questions, and I don’t think they necessarily have the same answer.

If you’re trying to predict what someone will say next, it helps to know what they’re talking about. It helps to track who did what to whom, what people believe, and what might happen next. So even though the training objective is defined over words, there’s a reason to expect models to learn something about the world that generated those words. The objective alone doesn’t tell us that they do, but it certainly doesn’t rule it out.

The question I find more useful is: what information does a particular model represent, and how does it use that information? Can it track a situation when we describe it in different ways? Can it distinguish a change in wording from a change in what actually happened? And does that representation support an appropriate inference in a new setting? Those are questions we can investigate experimentally.

So I’m wary of treating meaning as a single property that a system either has or doesn’t have. A model might represent some aspects of a situation quite well and fail completely on others. Understanding that pattern seems more productive than trying to settle the whole issue with a yes or no.

r002.rationale: The response distinguishes representations of described things from representations grounded in the world, but does not explain model-theoretic meaning in terms of possible worlds.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss proof-theoretic accounts or say that recognizing relationships between sentences can be sufficient for meaning.

r005.rationale: The response offers experimental questions about model representations, but does not state that making a conception of meaning precise generally makes it relatively straightforward to formulate a corresponding model question.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it helps to ask what we mean by “represent meaning,” because there are a few different questions hiding in there. One is whether a model captures something beyond the surface form of a sentence—whether it tracks who did what to whom, or that two very different sentences can describe the same situation. Another is whether those representations connect to the world in the way human language does. And a third is whether the model actually uses those representations when it produces an answer.

Those questions don’t necessarily have the same answer. A model trained only on text can learn a lot about the world, because text is produced by people talking about the world. But being able to extract some fact from a model’s internal state doesn’t, by itself, tell us that the model relies on that fact in a systematic way.

So I’m more interested in making the question concrete: what distinctions does the model represent, how do those representations support its behavior, and where do they break down? That seems more productive than trying to settle, all at once, whether it has meaning or doesn’t.
